items.title: Hermes Agent OS GitHub: Install Herald OS on Mac or Linux
items.content:
The Hermes Agent OS GitHub repo you want is iamlukethedev/Herald-OS — the free, open-source operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface. In the video below I show it running. This guide gives you the exact install commands for every platform, the requirements, and the gotchas to watch for.

Key takeaways

- The repo is github.com/iamlukethedev/Herald-OS (MIT licence).

- Mac: install Hermes, run `hermes setup`, then install the DMG from Releases.

- Linux: a Fedora-based ISO, an Arch package or a tarball.

- It’s 0.1 alpha — read the open issues first.

## The Hermes Agent OS GitHub repository

Herald OS lives at iamlukethedev/Herald-OS. It’s an independent project by Luke The Dev, released under the MIT licence, and it builds on Hermes Agent by Nous Research, which is also MIT. It isn’t affiliated with Nous. The project is very active — new pull requests land almost daily.

Herald OS at a glance

What it is
An agent-native operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface

Made by
Luke The Dev (iamlukethedev) — independent, not affiliated with Nous Research

Price
Free — MIT licence; you only pay for the AI model you connect

Version
0.1 alpha — early software

Platforms
macOS app (Apple Silicon, macOS 13+), Herald OS Linux (Fedora-based ISO), Arch/Omarchy package, Linux tarball

Needs
Hermes Agent, plus a Nous Portal account or an API key for a supported provider

Source
github.com/iamlukethedev/Herald-OS

## Install from the Hermes Agent OS GitHub on a Mac

For Apple Silicon Macs on macOS 13 or later, install Hermes Agent first:

```
curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash
source ~/.zshrc
hermes setup
```

Download the Herald OS DMG from the repo’s Releases page and drag it to Applications. The build isn’t notarised by Apple yet, so the README has you clear the quarantine flag:

```
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Herald OS.app"
```

Only do that for a DMG you downloaded from the official releases page. Intel Macs don’t have an app build — use the Linux VM instead.

Join the AI Profit Boardroom →Book a Free Strategy Session →

## Install on Linux, Arch or Omarchy

Arch Linux:

```
git clone https://github.com/iamlukethedev/Herald-OS.git
cd Herald-OS/packaging/arch/herald-os-bin
makepkg -si
herald-os setup
```

On Omarchy, after the Arch package, run `herald-os omarchy install`.

Other Linux distros use the tarball: verify the checksum, extract it to `/opt/herald-os`, run the bundled install script, then `herald-os setup`.

Herald OS Linux is a full Fedora-based system for 64-bit Intel/AMD PCs. Download both ISO parts, join them with `cat`, verify the SHA-256 checksum, write it to a USB stick of 8 GB or more, and boot from it. The developer notes it’s tested in a VM in CI but hasn’t been tried on much real hardware yet.

## Try it in a VM or build from source

On an Apple Silicon Mac you can try the Linux version in a virtual machine:

```
brew install qemu zstd
git clone https://github.com/iamlukethedev/Herald-OS.git && cd Herald-OS
bash linux/vm/try.sh
```

Allow about 20 GB of disk, 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM. To build the Mac app from source you need Node.js 22.12+, Git, Xcode Command Line Tools and Hermes Agent 0.21.3+, then:

```
npm run bootstrap
npm run dev
```

## Or let your AI agent install it

This is how I did it: I pasted the GitHub link into Claude and said “Can you set this up?” It was running about two minutes later. Ask your agent to follow the README for your platform and to stop and check with you before running anything with `sudo`.

## Hermes Agent OS GitHub: tips before you install

- Read the open issues — it’s alpha, and that’s where known bugs live.

- Use the official repo — not a fork or a re-upload.

- Verify checksums on the Linux downloads.

- Keep Hermes updated — source builds need 0.21.3 or later.

- Report bugs on GitHub — Luke ships fixes fast.

Once it’s running, my Herald OS review walks through the dashboard, spaces, missions and settings.

## What’s been changing in the repo

The project moves fast. Recent pull requests include:

- Tool scoping — Herald’s system tools now only run in Herald OS sessions, not your other Hermes sessions.

- Updater hardening — stops a Hermes session leaking into the backend or bridge.

- Filing documents by voice — a new skill for finding, reading, naming and filing documents.

- Safer Linux updates — update commands only act on Herald’s own image.

- Calendar access on Mac — the app now asks properly for calendar permission.

Watch or star the repo to get notified of new releases, and update regularly — in alpha software, fixes like these matter.

## Troubleshooting a Herald OS install

- “App is damaged” on Mac — that’s the missing notarisation; clear the quarantine flag as shown above.

- Hermes not found — run `source ~/.zshrc` or open a new terminal after installing Hermes.

- No model responding — run `hermes setup` again and check your provider.

- Connections not syncing — a known rough edge in my test; ask your agent to debug it or check the issues tab.

- Calendar not showing — grant calendar access when macOS asks.

## Getting started from the Hermes Agent OS GitHub repo

The Hermes Agent OS GitHub repo, iamlukethedev/Herald-OS, gives you a free, beautiful operating system for Hermes on Mac or Linux. Install Hermes, grab the release for your platform, keep approvals on, and you’re up and running.

If you hit a problem that isn’t covered above, search the repo’s issues for your exact error message first — with an alpha project, someone has often reported it already and a fix may be in the next release. If not, open a new issue with your platform, version and the steps to reproduce it. Clear bug reports help Luke ship fixes faster for everyone, and they’re the best way to give back to a free project like this.

Yes — it’s free and open source under the MIT licence. You only pay for the AI model you connect to Hermes.

items.title: Herald OS: The Free Hermes Agent Operating System, Tested
items.content:
Herald OS is a free, open-source, agent-native operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface — and honestly, it’s the best-looking way to use Hermes I’ve seen. You talk or type to Hermes, and it works across your whole machine. I set it up and gave you the full tour in the video below. Here’s what it does, how to get it, and how it compares with Hermes Desktop.

Key takeaways

- Herald OS is free and MIT-licensed, built by independent developer Luke The Dev.

- It wraps Hermes Agent in a full OS-style interface: dashboard, spaces, missions, memory, files and automations.

- It runs as a Mac app (Apple Silicon) or a full Linux system.

- It’s early alpha — brilliant design, a few rough edges.

## What Herald OS is

Herald OS describes itself as an agent-native operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface. Instead of opening apps and clicking around yourself, you tell Hermes what you want — open an app, sort your files, run a routine — and it does it, asking permission before it changes anything.

It’s built by Luke The Dev, who posts loads of Hermes content on X. Shout out to Luke — this is a seriously impressive project. It’s independent, not made by Nous Research, but it runs on Hermes Agent, which is installed alongside it.

Herald OS at a glance

What it is
An agent-native operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface

Made by
Luke The Dev (iamlukethedev) — independent, not affiliated with Nous Research

Price
Free — MIT licence; you only pay for the AI model you connect

Version
0.1 alpha — early software

Platforms
macOS app (Apple Silicon, macOS 13+), Herald OS Linux (Fedora-based ISO), Arch/Omarchy package, Linux tarball

Needs
Hermes Agent, plus a Nous Portal account or an API key for a supported provider

Source
github.com/iamlukethedev/Herald-OS

## How I set up Herald OS

I literally opened Claude and said, “Can you set this up?” About two minutes later, Herald OS was running. If you’d rather do it yourself, the steps for every platform are in my Herald OS GitHub install guide.

Why bother with an operating system for your agent? Because it makes Hermes far easier to navigate and command. When Hermes first came out, back around March or April, we all ran it in the terminal and it was messy. A proper interface changes how much you actually use it.

Want this working in your business, not just bookmarked? Setting up an agent operating system for your business is exactly what we build together inside the AI Profit Boardroom — 3,400+ members, four live calls a week, and a full one-hour DeepSeek Harness course in the classroom.

Prefer it mapped 1-on-1 first? Book a free strategy session and we’ll plan it for your exact situation.

Join the AI Profit Boardroom →Book a Free Strategy Session →

## A tour of the Herald OS dashboard

When you open it, it says “Good morning, Julian — your day already in motion.” It pulls in your scheduled tasks for the day, shows what needs attention, and suggests where to pick up where you left off, based on your recent documents, projects, chats and calendar events. You can switch that on or off. You can talk to it with your voice, and it even used screenshots I’d recently taken on my desktop to show what I’ve been working on.

Section
What it does

Overview
Your day at a glance: scheduled tasks, what needs attention, and up to three “pick up where you left off” suggestions

Hermes
Chat with Hermes normally, with a preview pane and sources Hermes can read

Spaces
Separate Ideas, Work and Personal spaces — add more for clients or companies

Missions
Give Hermes a goal and it plans it out step by step

Memory
See and manage everything Hermes remembers about you

Files
Recent, favourites, projects, downloads, shared and deleted files Hermes can access

Automations
Switch scheduled routines on and off

Connections
Bring apps and tools into your agents

Settings
Models, where agents run (including Docker), background agents, approvals, history, themes, plugins, voice and privacy

Herald OS is an independent project by Luke The Dev that puts Hermes Agent at the centre of your computer. You don’t open apps and click through menus — you tell Hermes what you need, and it does the work across the machine.

## How the Hermes Herald AI agent controls your computer

Herald OS connects to Hermes through a plugin called `herald-os-bridge`, which gives Hermes a set of system tools. Each tool has a permission tier:

Tool tier
What happens

Read
Runs directly and is logged

Act
Runs directly and is logged

Mutate
Asks you first

Destructive
Asks you every single time

Every action is written to an audit log, so you can always see what your agent did. The developer has also tightened things so Herald’s system tools only run inside Herald OS sessions — not in your other Hermes sessions like messaging or cron jobs.

## Talking to Hermes in Herald OS

Voice is one of the most useful parts. Use a push-to-talk key or say “hey Hermes”, and choose between a free voice engine and an opt-in real-time one. It feels like having Jarvis on your computer. There’s a full list of voice commands in Settings, and the latest update lets you find, read, name and file documents by voice — perfect for sorting a folder of badly named PDFs.

## Memory, files and spaces

- Memory — see everything Hermes remembers about you, and manage it.

- Files — control exactly which files Hermes can access.

- Spaces — keep Ideas, Work and Personal separate, and add spaces for each client or company.

- Automations — your scheduled routines, switched on and off in one place, synced with Hermes Desktop.

Careful when you screen-share: my Memory page showed my Telegram details while recording. Check what’s visible before you share your screen.

## Setting up the Hermes Herald AI agent safely

- Start with auto-approve off and “ask before sending messages” on.

- Limit background agents until you know what’s running.

- Check the activity history regularly — it’s easy to forget what you set up.

- Give Hermes access to the folders it needs, not your whole drive.

- Remember it’s alpha software — keep backups of anything important.

For the full install steps, see my Herald OS GitHub guide, and for the overall tour, my Herald OS review.

Hermes in Herald OS
Hermes Desktop

Made by
Luke The Dev (independent)
Nous Research (official)

Scope
Runs your whole computer — apps, files, system settings
An app for chatting with and configuring Hermes

Organisation
Spaces, missions, a daily dashboard
Profiles, chats, plugin catalogue

Voice
Push-to-talk, “hey Hermes”, free or real-time engine
Via voice plugins

Maturity
0.1 alpha
Stable releases

The big difference is scope. Hermes Desktop is where you talk to your agent; in Herald OS, Hermes is the computer’s front door. You can run both — my automations showed up in each.

- “Prep my day” — check my calendar and what’s scheduled, then tell me what needs attention.

- “Sort my Downloads folder and rename the PDFs properly.”

- “Set up a daily 6am to-do recap.”

- “Start a mission: build a landing page for my new offer.”

- “Explain why that app just crashed.”

- “Switch to my Work space and open my latest project.”

Start with read-only requests while you learn how it behaves, then move on to ones that change things once you’re comfortable with the approval prompts.

If you already use Hermes, this is the most natural way I’ve seen to let it run your computer: clean design, sensible permissions and voice built in. The Hermes Herald AI agent setup is free — try it, keep approvals on, and build from there.

One last tip: treat Hermes in Herald OS like a new team member. Give it small, clear jobs first, check its work in the activity history, and widen its permissions only as it earns your trust. That approach has worked for every agent I’ve set up, and it’s the fastest way to get real value without nasty surprises.
